newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Careworn Romanians will vote with economy in mind.
newsitem.headline: Careworn Romanians will vote with economy in mind.

text.p: Careworn Romanians, still trapped in poverty seven years after the fall of communism, vote on Sunday for a government and president to guide them into the next century.
President Ion Iliescu, in power since the execution of Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu in 1989, hopes voters will trust his blend of paternalism and cautious reform and keep him in office.

Opinion polls favour him, but his main rivals -- academic Emil Constantinescu and ex-premier Petre Roman -- have gained ground recently and most expect a second round of voting later in the month will be needed to decide who leads the country.

If Iliescu wins he may face a hostile coalition government. His Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), made up of ex-communist functionaries, is mired in corruption scandals and running behind Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR) bloc.

Polls open at 6 a.m. (0400 GMT) and officially close at 9 p.m. (1900 GMT), but could be kept open until midnight to cope with a late surge of voters. Exit polls will quickly follow the end of voting. Official results are due late on Monday.

Many of the 17 million voters appear disgusted at soaring prices, charges of ruling party incompetence and an economic slump that has pushed living standards well below those of near neighbours Hungary, Poland, and the Czech Republic.
Romania is the only eastern European country where non-communists have not yet been in office.

To form the ground-breaking government, the centrist CDR will need to ally with Roman's Social Democratic Union (USD). Both parties promise quicker economic reforms and an end to abuse of power, but disputes have so far kept them apart.

Iliescu, who easily won elections in 1990 and 1992, has portrayed himself as a bulwark of stability. He points to the steep economic decline and conflicts in neighbouring Bulgaria and Yugoslavia as pitfalls to be avoided.

"Romania has achieved profound but cautious change. We have lived modestly but with the certainty of what will happen tomorrow," he told a television debate this week with all 16 presidential candidates.
Voters say their main concerns are economic. With average monthly wages below $100 and a decaying industrial system workers complain of poverty and insecurity.
Good weather forecast across the country may encourage a high turnout -- a factor that favours Iliescu, who is popular in rural areas but has lost support among industrial workers.

Romanian media spent Saturday exhorting voters to exercise their democratic rights. A 48-hour pre-vote campaigning pause left television stations running programmes explaining the mechanics of the voting system.

Romanian voters mark ballot papers with rubber stamps -- ink ran out in some place in this year's local elections -- and will choose 341 politicians to sit in the lower Chamber of Deputies and 143 for the upper house, the Senate.
Winners receive a four-year mandate in the election, which is being carefully scrutinised for fraud by opposition groups.

Commercial PRO-TV television highlighted some whom the system has failed. It said hundreds of orphans who lack birth certificates and still live in grisly Ceausescu-era blocks do not have the identity papers they need to cast their votes.
